claim: Palestine was an Arab country stolen by outsiders.

heard.who: Fayez Sayegh, Palestine Liberation Organization Research Center, "Zionist Colonialism in Palestine" (1965)
heard.quote: the establishment of a colonial Zionist state in the Afro-Asian bridge, the Arab land of Palestine

answer: Two things are true. Arabs were the large majority of the population under the Mandate (78 percent Muslim in the 1922 census), and earlier. But no independent state called Palestine, governed by its Arab inhabitants, existed before 1948. The land was ruled from outside in this order: the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, Assyria, Babylon, Persia (539-332 BCE), Alexander and the Ptolemies and Seleucids, the Hasmoneans (to 63 BCE), Rome and Byzantium, the Arab caliphates from the 630s, the Crusaders (1099-1187), the Ayyubids and Mamluks, the Ottomans (1516/17-1917), and Britain (1917-1948). Many rulers were Muslim or Arab; many were not. Who ruled when does not settle who has rights today.

facts.text: Persia ruled the land from 539 BCE until Alexander in 332 BCE; Judah was the province of Yehud, with considerable internal autonomy.

facts.text: Alexander the Great conquered the land in 332 BCE; Ptolemaic Egypt held it from 301 to about 200 BCE.

facts.text: The Hasmonean dynasty ruled Judea as a Jewish state from the 140s BCE until Pompey's intervention in 63 BCE.

facts.text: Rome took control in 63 BCE, ruled through client kings, annexed Judea in 6 CE, and renamed the province Syria Palaestina after 135 CE.

facts.text: Byzantine (Eastern Roman) rule followed, with the provinces of Palaestina Prima, Secunda and Tertia from the late 4th century; Persia held Jerusalem briefly in the early 7th century.

facts.text: Arab Muslim armies conquered the land in the 630s (635-638); Rashidun, Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid caliphates then ruled it, with the Seljuk Turks briefly in the late 11th century.

facts.text: European Crusaders held the Kingdom of Jerusalem from 1099 to 1187, with a reduced Crusader presence until the Mamluks took Acre in 1291.

facts.text: The Ayyubids (1187-1260) and then the Mamluks (1260-1517) ruled the land from Egypt and Damascus.

facts.text: Arabs (Muslims and Christians) were the large majority of the population: in the 1922 census 78 percent were Muslims, about 11 percent Jews and about 9 percent Christians.

sources.title: 1922 Census of Palestine
sources.quote: The total population of Palestine was given as 757,182, of whom 590,890 (78%) were Muslims

sources.title: The British Army in Palestine
sources.quote: Mandatory Palestine had a majority Arab population

contested: Whether Arabs were the majority "for many centuries" is not settled by one source: Ottoman and early Mandate counts are disputed, and the 1922 census may have undercounted Bedouin. This card relies on the 1922 census for the one sure figure.

Historians differ on which rulers count as "native": Arab-speaking Muslims governed from Damascus, Baghdad or Cairo under the caliphates, but those capitals were not in Palestine. Some call that Arab rule of the land; others call it rule by an empire that included it.
The kingdom of David and Solomon and the date of the Babylonian destruction (587 or 586 BCE) are disputed.
Crusader and Ayyubid frontiers moved; the dates 1187 and 1291 mark the main changes, not a clean line.
could_not_verify: The Crusader and Ayyubid-Mamluk facts rest on one readable reliable source (a Biblical Archaeology Society chronology page); Britannica, Taylor & Francis and worldhistory.org pages could not be read by the checker.
The Assyrian conquest of Samaria has two readable reliable sources; dates for its fall (722 or 720 BCE) differ.

The Byzantine, caliphate and Arab-majority facts have two or fewer readable reliable sources. I did not find a source I could read for the population before 1922 beyond estimates cited in pages the checker cannot read.
The no-independent-state fact is partly an inference from the list of rulers; it relies on the Ottoman and Mandate sources, not on a single statement of it.
not_claimed: This card does not claim that who ruled when settles who has rights today, or that long rule gives or removes a claim.
It does not say the Arab majority had no claim, or that a Jewish minority had none.
It does not say Arabs never ruled the land: caliphs, Fatimids, Ayyubids and Mamluks were Muslim rulers of it, some Arab, some not.
It does not say the land was empty or that its inhabitants were absent.
